title: US Section 301 investigations into Singapore's industrial capacity and forced labour
asked: MPs asked about the US Section 301 investigations that include Singapore: the basis for Singapore's inclusion, whether sectors could face tariffs, the reported US$27 billion trade figure, forced labour scrutiny, and what engagement and support is under way.
asked_by: Mr Alex Yam, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
response: Ms Gan Siow Huang said the US Trade Representative began two Section 301 investigations on 11 and 12 March 2026, one covering 16 economies on structural excess capacity and one covering 60 economies on forced labour, and that Singapore is subject to both. She said MTI had corrected the USTR's Federal Register Notice, which had stated Singapore ran a US$27 billion surplus with the US in 2024, and the USTR has since removed that statement. She said it would be premature to comment on the basis or outcomes of the investigations or their impact on export sectors, that the 10% Section 122 tariff on Singapore's exports to the US since 24 February 2026 is unchanged, and that the Government will keep engaging the US and helping companies diversify markets. She also said Singapore criminalises forced labour under domestic laws and that the Government will attend the USTR public hearings.

key_points.point: Two Section 301 investigations were initiated on 11 and 12 March 2026: one covering 16 economies on structural excess capacity, the other covering 60 economies on forced labour, with Singapore subject to both.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: On 11 and 12 March 2026, the Office of the US Trade Representative initiated two investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

key_points.point: MTI clarified that it was the US, not Singapore, that ran a US$27 billion trade surplus with Singapore in 2024, and the USTR removed the inaccurate statement from its Federal Register Notice.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: it was the US which ran a trade surplus of US$27 billion with Singapore in 2024

key_points.point: The 10% Section 122 tariff on Singapore's exports to the US, in place since 24 February 2026, remains unchanged.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: the Section 122 tariff of 10% imposed on Singapore's exports to the US since 24 February 2026 remains unchanged

key_points.point: The Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce will keep gathering feedback on how businesses are affected and address specific concerns as they arise.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: The Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce will continue to gather feedback on how businesses are affected and address specific concerns as they arise.

key_points.point: A Business Adaptation Grant remains available to help companies understand the implications of the US tariffs on their businesses.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: there is a Business Adaptation Grant, which remains available to help companies understand the implications of the US tariffs on their businesses

key_points.point: The US has not given Singapore reasons for including it in the Section 301 investigations.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: the US has not given us reasons on why they have included Singapore under the Section 301 investigations

key_points.point: Singapore criminalises forced labour under laws including the Penal Code and the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act, and it is prohibited under the Constitution.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: we also criminalise forced labour in Singapore under various laws, including the Penal Code and the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act

key_points.point: Singapore has been and will continue to strengthen diversification of its trade linkages.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: Singapore has been and will continue to strengthen the diversification of our trade linkages

key_points.point: Companies are not required to participate in the USTR public hearings, but are encouraged to give feedback to MTI so it can represent them.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: they are not required to participate in the hearings

key_points.point: The Government will attend the USTR public hearings.
key_points.speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
key_points.quote: The answer is yes; we will be attending the hearings.

left_open: Which specific sectors may face heightened scrutiny or trade risks
Whether domestic sectors reliant on migrant workers may face increased scrutiny
Whether any early shifts in investment decisions or supply chain strategies have been observed
Whether traditional indicators of trade imbalance are no longer the primary basis for such investigations, and what precedent this sets for small open economies
supplementary: Reasons for Singapore's inclusion, trade diversification, support for firms, forced labour scrutiny and whether Singapore will attend the USTR hearings
